title: Short Lighting
description: Short lighting in short lighting terms keys the side of the face turned away from camera, so the camera sees more shadow than light. The head looks slimmer and more dimensional because the near cheek falls off.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Mystery sits on the camera side. We look at the dark plane and infer the person from the far, lit cheek.
Noir portraits and serious close-ups use it so a face is sculpted instead of presented like a passport photo. It is the wrong tool when a comic or public figure should feel open to us.
Short is not a shadow pattern by itself: you can light short as Rembrandt, loop, or even a soft wrap. The definition is which cheek faces the lens, not the nose shadow.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Turn the face so the far cheek takes the key (often 45 to 90 degrees from camera). The near cheek, the one occupying more of the frame, goes toward shadow.
Hardness can be hard for noir or medium for drama. Color follows the key source.

Combine with a low fill so the near eye does not die unless you want it to. Prompt: Short lighting on [Subject], the side turned away from camera is keyed, the near side falls toward shadow, slimming and dramatic.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it to sculpt a face and put mystery on the camera side, a close-up in an office or a night bar. Do not use it when the character is presenting themselves to the public in a broad, open way.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Broad lighting keys the camera-facing cheek, the reverse. Rembrandt lighting is a triangle pattern often shot short, but Rembrandt can be broad if the triangle is on the near cheek.
Split lighting is a 90-degree cut that is usually short if the dark half faces us. Side lighting describes direction, not which cheek is near camera.
Broad LightingOpen, readable, less mystery.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: Portrait noir and Godfather-adjacent close-ups often key the far cheek so the camera sits with the shadow. Road to Perdition does the same sculpting in dark interiors.
Read the near cheek: if it is the dark one, you are short.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Name which cheek is near. Use: "Short lighting on [Subject], the side turned away from camera is keyed, the near side falls toward shadow, slimming and dramatic." Add that the camera-facing cheek is the darker one.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is broad lighting or a frontal butterfly. The tell is a bright near cheek filling the frame.
Fix it by turning the face or swinging the key onto the far side.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is short lighting in film?
Lighting the side of the face turned away from camera so the near, camera-facing cheek falls toward shadow. It slims and adds dimension.
Short lighting vs broad lighting
Short keys the far cheek; the camera sees more shadow. Broad keys the near cheek; the camera sees more light.
When should I use short lighting?
Use it to sculpt a face and keep mystery on the camera side. Skip it for open, public, comic portraits.
How do I prompt short lighting for AI image or video?
State that the side turned away from camera is keyed and the near cheek falls toward shadow. Mention a slimming, dimensional face.
